technical_body.purpose: Bell system's automated pre-payment platform for coin-toll transactions. Removed operators from most coin-toll calls; the payphone reports coin deposits to the toll switch via in-band tones.

coin_tones.dime_66ms: two 66 ms bursts separated by 66 ms
coin_tones.quarter_33ms: five 33 ms bursts separated by 33 ms
coin_tones.dollar_650ms: one 650 ms burst (rare, not universally implemented)

technical_body.path: 1700+2200 Hz coin-tones injected by the payphone's coin-signal generator onto the 4-wire toll trunk; the toll switch's coin-signal receiver credits the deposit.
technical_body.attack_surface: The red-box attack. Any tone generator emitting the 1700+2200 Hz pair with correct pulse timing will be credited by an ACTS receiver, regardless of whether a coin was actually deposited. Receivers tolerated ±10-20% timing slop, so both the GR-506 66/33 ms spec and Phrack 33.9's 60/35 ms homebrew timing worked.
technical_body.died_because: 1) T1/robbed-bit trunks stripped in-band ACTS supervision from the coin-signal path. 2) Bell 1C/1D single-slot payphones were retrofitted or replaced by 'smart' phones with local coin validation (Millennium, COCOT) starting mid-90s. 3) RBOC divestitures of payphone operations 2000-2007 accelerated retirement. 4) By 2002 red box attacks were largely inert in North America.

technical_body.purpose: The Western Electric single-slot payphone that replaced the older three-slot design. Coin escrow, magnetic sensor, and coin-tone oscillator all in one armored steel housing.
technical_body.coin_validation: electromagnetic sensor detects coin size + composition; oscillator emits ACTS tone bursts to the toll switch
technical_body.coin_control: TSPS operator or ACTS can send coin-collect / coin-return signals back to the phone; a local coin relay routes the escrowed coin into the vault or the return chute.
technical_body.attack_surface_summary: The prototypical red-box target. Because coin validation ran the tone up to the toll switch, injecting synthesized 1700+2200 Hz tones bypassed the coin sensor entirely.
technical_body.died_because: Retrofitted with locally-validating smart terminals 1996-2001; by 2001 most Bell single-slots were retired or converted. Physical fortress-phone housings remained in service as chassis for the replacement smart electronics for another few years.

technical_body.purpose: Nortel's DSP-based smart payphone. Local coin validation via optical + mass sensor; generates ACTS-look-alike tones internally for backward compatibility with any legacy monitoring, but the tones are ceremonial — the actual coin decision is local.
technical_body.coin_validation: local, in the payphone's own DSP + optical/mass sensor. Deposits are recorded before any tone is sent.
technical_body.signaling_to_CO: Standard POTS loop + DTMF for dialing. Management link back to the 'Millennium Manager' central server via periodic modem call to a maintenance number.
technical_body.attack_surface: Immune to red-boxing — the receiver is local, not on the toll switch. Attack surface shifted to the maintenance modem interface and to physical/vault attacks on the phone itself. Common in Canada (Bell Canada deployed Millennium heavily) and select US Bell operating companies.
technical_body.died_because: Not fully retired — some Millennium phones remain in service as of 2026. Payphones overall are largely gone due to mobile ubiquity, not to attacks on Millennium specifically.

technical_body.purpose: Non-Bell-owned payphone — installed by a private operator (bar, hotel lobby, laundromat, gas station) on a plain residential POTS loop. Validates coins LOCALLY; the CO sees only a subscriber-loop origination.
technical_body.signaling_to_CO: Ordinary POTS loop; no ACTS supervision. From the CO's viewpoint the COCOT is a subscriber, not a coin phone.
technical_body.coin_validation: local, in the COCOT's own electronics — never on the toll switch. This is why red-boxing never worked against COCOTs.

service_mode_attack.entry: dial the phone's own number, then enter a 4-digit password
capabilities_once_inside: dial out on the trunk the phone answered on (variant of the diverter attack applied to the payphone chassis)

technical_body.phreak_relevance: COCOTs became phreak-visible in the mid-1990s — the default admin passwords made them soft targets even without red-box tones. Discussed extensively in Phrack 48 (COCOT Frequencies) and 2600 Spring 1994 (The COCOT Files).

name: TSPS / TOPS / OSPS operator-attended coin handling

technical_body.purpose: The operator platform behind coin/toll/collect operations that ACTS didn't handle. TSPS = Traffic Service Position System (Western Electric, 1969). Later succeeded by TOPS (Nortel DMS-based) and OSPS (5ESS-based).
operator_functions: emergency interrupt (bridge into any active call)
technical_body.coin_control_signals_from_operator_side: coin collect 700+1100 Hz for 900 ms, coin return 1100+1700 Hz for 900 ms, ringback 700+1700 Hz — see green_coin_collect / green_coin_return records
technical_body.attack_surface: Green-box: spoof the coin-collect / coin-return tones from the caller side to make the payphone believe the operator has released it. Rarely worked in practice — the operator platform normally sent these tones from the toll switch toward the coin phone, and injecting them into the calling loop only succeeded in specific four-wire topologies with poor filtering.
technical_body.died_because: Digital operator platforms (TOPS on DMS, OSPS on 5ESS) migrated coin control to out-of-band messaging; the standalone operator tones survived but the phreak-relevant injection paths closed.

technical_body.purpose: The pre-ACTS three-slot Western Electric payphone. Distinct coin slots for nickel, dime, quarter; each coin triggered a mechanical bell or gong that the operator listened for (one gong = nickel, two = dime, one long = quarter).
technical_body.coin_validation: operator-attended — the operator heard the gong pattern over the line and manually credited the deposit before completing the call
technical_body.phreak_relevance_historic: The predecessor era to the red box. Some phreaks recorded the bell/gong patterns and played them into the mouthpiece; effective against inattentive operators in the 1960s. This is the origin of the phrase 'coin box' attack.
technical_body.died_because: Replaced by Bell 1C/1D single-slot fortress phones starting 1965; last widespread three-slot units retired by mid-1970s.
